categories.label: Analytics
categories.description: Web analytics, product analytics, and visitor tracking

entries.name: Plausible

fields.Resource: medium (~512MB — ClickHouse is the main consumer)

prose: Lightweight, privacy-friendly web analytics. No cookies, fully GDPR/CCPA/PECR compliant out of the box. Single-page dashboard shows top pages, referrers, countries, devices, and goals — nothing more. Script is under 1 KB.
entries.pick: you want dead-simple, privacy-respecting web analytics with a clean UI and no cookie banners needed.

alternatives.name: Umami
alternatives.text: Both are privacy-first and lightweight. Plausible uses ClickHouse (better at scale), has goal/funnel tracking, and revenue attribution. Umami is simpler to deploy (single DB) and MIT-licensed.

alternatives.name: Matomo
alternatives.text: Plausible is minimalist and opinionated; Matomo is a full GA replacement with heatmaps, session recordings, and A/B testing. Choose Plausible for simplicity, Matomo for feature parity with Google Analytics.

alternatives.name: PostHog
alternatives.text: Different categories. Plausible is web analytics (pageviews, referrers). PostHog is product analytics (funnels, cohorts, feature flags, session replay). Use Plausible for marketing sites, PostHog for SaaS products.

entries.name: Umami
prose: Simple, fast, privacy-first analytics. Cookie-free, GDPR-compliant. Tracks pageviews, referrers, browsers, OS, devices, countries, and custom events. Multi-site support with team accounts. Clean UI with real-time dashboard.
entries.pick: you want the simplest possible self-hosted analytics — one container, one database, MIT license, done.

alternatives.name: Plausible
alternatives.text: Umami is lighter to deploy (no ClickHouse), MIT-licensed, and has multi-site built in. Plausible has richer goal/funnel tracking and scales better with ClickHouse. Both are privacy-first.

alternatives.name: Matomo
alternatives.text: Umami is minimalist (pageviews + events). Matomo gives you session recordings, heatmaps, form analytics, tag manager, and full GA-level reporting. Umami wins on simplicity and resource use.

alternatives.name: PostHog
alternatives.text: Umami tracks website visits; PostHog tracks product behavior. No overlap — you could run both (Umami for your blog, PostHog for your app).

entries.name: Matomo
prose: Full-featured Google Analytics alternative with 20+ years of development. Supports goals, funnels, ecommerce tracking, custom dimensions, heatmaps (paid plugin), session recordings (paid plugin), A/B testing, tag manager, and roll-up reporting. Import historical GA data. GDPR-compliant with optional cookie consent.
entries.pick: you need a complete GA replacement with enterprise features — ecommerce tracking, custom reports, import from GA, and a mature plugin ecosystem.

alternatives.name: Plausible
alternatives.text: Matomo has 10x more features (tag manager, heatmaps, ecommerce, custom reports). Plausible is intentionally minimal. Matomo needs more maintenance and resources.

alternatives.name: Umami
alternatives.text: Matomo is the "full suite" where Umami is the "just pageviews" tool. Matomo if you're migrating from GA and need feature parity; Umami if you want something simple.

alternatives.name: PostHog
alternatives.text: Overlapping but different focus. Matomo is web analytics (pageviews, conversions, SEO). PostHog is product analytics (user journeys, feature flags, experiments). Matomo for marketing teams; PostHog for product teams.

entries.name: PostHog

fields.Resource: heavy (~2GB+ — requires PostgreSQL, Redis, ClickHouse, Kafka)

prose: All-in-one product analytics suite. Event tracking, funnels, user paths, cohort analysis, session replay, feature flags, A/B experiments, surveys, and data warehouse queries. Autocapture means minimal instrumentation. Built for product teams who want to understand user behavior end-to-end.
entries.pick: you're building a SaaS/product and want unified analytics, feature flags, session replay, and experimentation in one platform — and you have the resources to run it.

alternatives.name: Plausible
alternatives.text: PostHog is product analytics (funnels, retention, experiments). Plausible is website analytics (pageviews, referrers). Different tools for different jobs. Many teams run both.

alternatives.name: Umami
alternatives.text: PostHog is orders of magnitude more complex. Umami gives you page-level stats in 5 minutes. PostHog gives you product intelligence in a few hours of setup and 2 GB of RAM.

alternatives.name: Matomo
alternatives.text: PostHog has feature flags, experiments, and session replay built-in. Matomo has stronger traditional web analytics (SEO, ecommerce). PostHog for product-led teams; Matomo for marketing-led teams.

categories.label: Automation
categories.description: Workflow automation, job scheduling, and integration platforms

entries.name: n8n

fields.Backup: snapshot `/home/node/.n8n` or export workflows as JSON
fields.License: FSL-1.1-Apache-2.0 (source-available, converts to Apache-2.0 after 2 years)

prose: Visual workflow automation platform with 400+ integrations. Build complex automations using a node-based canvas editor — connect triggers, logic, APIs, databases, and AI models. Supports code nodes (JavaScript/Python), webhooks, cron schedules, and error handling with retries.
entries.pick: you want the most polished visual workflow builder with deep integrations, code-when-needed flexibility, and a large community sharing templates.

alternatives.name: Node-RED
alternatives.text: n8n focuses on business/SaaS integrations with a modern UI; Node-RED is lower-level and better for IoT/hardware/protocol wiring.

alternatives.name: Activepieces
alternatives.text: n8n has more integrations and a mature ecosystem; Activepieces is fully MIT and simpler for non-developers.

alternatives.name: Huginn
alternatives.text: n8n has a visual editor and pre-built connectors; Huginn is code-first with more granular agent scheduling.

entries.name: Node-RED
prose: Flow-based programming tool originally from IBM for wiring IoT devices, APIs, and online services. Drag-and-drop nodes in a browser-based editor — supports MQTT, HTTP, WebSocket, TCP, serial, GPIO, and custom function nodes (JavaScript). Huge community palette with 4000+ contributed nodes.
entries.pick: you need IoT/hardware integration, protocol bridging (MQTT, Modbus, OPC-UA), or lightweight event-driven flows with minimal overhead.

alternatives.name: n8n
alternatives.text: Node-RED is better for IoT/protocol/hardware; n8n is better for SaaS-to-SaaS business workflows.

alternatives.name: Activepieces
alternatives.text: Node-RED is more technical and flexible; Activepieces is easier for non-developers building app integrations.

alternatives.name: Huginn
alternatives.text: Node-RED has a visual flow editor and real-time debugging; Huginn focuses on scheduled web-scraping agents.

entries.name: Activepieces
prose: Open-source Zapier/Make alternative with a clean, no-code visual builder. 200+ pieces (integrations) covering popular SaaS apps, with triggers, actions, and branching logic. Supports custom pieces in TypeScript, webhook triggers, and scheduled flows.
entries.pick: you want a Zapier-like experience that's fully self-hosted, MIT-licensed, and friendly for non-technical team members.

alternatives.name: n8n
alternatives.text: Activepieces is simpler and fully MIT; n8n has more integrations and a source-available license.

alternatives.name: Node-RED
alternatives.text: Activepieces is easier for business users; Node-RED is better for technical/IoT use cases.

alternatives.name: Huginn
alternatives.text: Activepieces has a modern no-code UI; Huginn is more powerful for custom scraping/agent logic but harder to set up.

entries.name: Huginn
prose: System of programmable agents that monitor the web and act on your behalf. Agents can scrape websites, watch for changes, parse RSS/JSON, send notifications, trigger webhooks, and chain together in directed graphs with scheduling. Think IFTTT meets cron meets web scraping — all self-hosted.
entries.pick: you need scheduled web scraping, change detection, or complex multi-step agent pipelines where you want fine-grained control over timing and data flow.

alternatives.name: n8n
alternatives.text: Huginn excels at scheduled scraping/monitoring agents; n8n is better for interactive workflows with SaaS integrations.

alternatives.name: Node-RED
alternatives.text: Huginn is built around scheduled agents and web data; Node-RED is event-driven and better for real-time IoT flows.

alternatives.name: Activepieces
alternatives.text: Huginn offers more power for custom scraping logic; Activepieces is easier to use for standard app-to-app automations.

categories.label: Backup
categories.description: Backup solutions, snapshot tools, and disaster recovery

entries.name: Restic

fields.Config: env vars + CLI flags (no config file)
fields.Backup: repository is the backup (local, S3, SFTP, rclone, REST)

prose: Fast, secure, cross-platform backup program. Encrypts and deduplicates data at the chunk level. Supports dozens of storage backends via rclone integration. No daemon — run via cron or systemd timers.
entries.pick: you want a simple, fast CLI backup tool with excellent dedup, encryption by default, and broad backend support (S3, B2, SFTP, local, rclone).

alternatives.name: BorgBackup
alternatives.text: Restic has more native backends (S3, B2, Azure, GCS) and better Windows support. Borg has better compression and slightly better dedup ratios. Restic is simpler to set up for cloud targets.

alternatives.name: Duplicati
alternatives.text: Restic is CLI-only and scriptable; Duplicati has a GUI for less technical users. Restic is faster and more reliable for large datasets.

alternatives.name: Kopia
alternatives.text: Both are fast Go-based tools with similar backends. Kopia adds a built-in web UI, policies, and snapshot mounting. Restic is more battle-tested with a larger community.

entries.name: BorgBackup

fields.Image: N/A (no official container; community images exist)

prose: Deduplicating archiver with compression and authenticated encryption. Excellent space efficiency via content-defined chunking. Append-only mode for tamper resistance. Primarily targets local and SSH-accessible storage.
entries.pick: you want the best deduplication and compression ratios for local or SSH-based backup targets, and you value a mature, well-audited codebase.

alternatives.name: Restic
alternatives.text: Borg has better compression (lz4/zstd/lzma) and slightly better dedup. Restic supports more backends natively (S3, B2) without extra tooling. Borg requires SSH access to remote repos.

alternatives.name: Duplicati
alternatives.text: Borg is CLI-only with better performance and reliability. Duplicati provides a web GUI and native cloud support but has a history of database corruption issues on large backups.

alternatives.name: Kopia
alternatives.text: Borg is older and proven; Kopia is newer with built-in cloud backends, GUI, and policies. Borg's dedup is slightly more space-efficient; Kopia is faster on large repos.

entries.name: Duplicati

fields.Backup: targets 30+ cloud backends (S3, B2, Google Drive, OneDrive, SFTP, WebDAV)

prose: Encrypted cloud backup with a web-based GUI. Supports incremental backups, scheduling, and email notifications. Targets virtually any cloud or local storage. AES-256 encryption before upload.
entries.pick: you want a GUI-driven backup tool that non-technical users can manage, with broad cloud storage support out of the box.

alternatives.name: Restic
alternatives.text: Duplicati has a GUI and built-in scheduler; Restic is CLI-only but faster and more reliable at scale. Duplicati has had historical database corruption bugs on very large backup sets.

alternatives.name: BorgBackup
alternatives.text: Duplicati supports cloud backends natively and has a web UI. Borg is more reliable and space-efficient but SSH-only for remote targets.

alternatives.name: Kopia
alternatives.text: Both have GUIs. Kopia is faster, has better dedup, and is more actively developed. Duplicati supports more obscure cloud backends and has been around longer.

entries.name: Kopia

fields.Backup: repository is the backup (local, S3, B2, GCS, Azure, SFTP, rclone, WebDAV)

prose: Fast encrypted backup tool with built-in web UI and CLI. Content-addressable deduplication, compression (zstd), and client-side encryption. Policy-based retention, snapshot browsing, and FUSE/WebDAV mounting of snapshots.
entries.pick: you want the speed and scriptability of Restic plus a built-in web UI, snapshot policies, and native multi-backend support — essentially a modern all-in-one.

alternatives.name: Restic
alternatives.text: Kopia adds a web UI, policy engine, snapshot mounting, and server mode. Restic has a larger community and longer track record. Performance is comparable; Kopia edges ahead on large repos.

alternatives.name: BorgBackup
alternatives.text: Kopia has native cloud backends and a GUI; Borg is SSH-only but has better compression ratios. Kopia is faster for initial backups.

alternatives.name: Duplicati
alternatives.text: Kopia is significantly faster, more reliable, and has better dedup. Duplicati supports a few more exotic backends but Kopia covers all mainstream ones.

categories.label: Calendar & CRM
categories.description: Calendar servers, scheduling tools, and customer relationship management

entries.name: Radicale

fields.Auth: htpasswd, LDAP (via plugin), reverse proxy header, PAM

prose: A minimal CalDAV and CardDAV server written in Python. Stores calendars and contacts as flat files on the filesystem — no database required. Designed to be simple to install, configure, and maintain. Supports file-based storage with git versioning via plugins, flexible authentication, and fine-grained access control via rights files.
entries.pick: you want the simplest possible CalDAV/CardDAV server with near-zero resource usage and file-based storage you can easily back up and version-control.

alternatives.name: Baikal
alternatives.text: Radicale is lighter (no PHP/web server needed) and stores data as plain files. Baikal has a friendlier web admin UI for managing users and calendars, and uses a database (SQLite/MySQL). Choose Radicale if you prefer filesystem storage and minimal dependencies.

alternatives.name: Cal.com
alternatives.text: Completely different purposes. Radicale is a calendar/contacts data server (CalDAV/CardDAV); Cal.com is a scheduling/booking platform. Use Radicale to sync your calendar across devices; use Cal.com to let others book time with you.

alternatives.name: Twenty
alternatives.text: No overlap. Radicale serves calendars and contacts; Twenty is a CRM for managing customer relationships and pipelines.

entries.name: Baikal
prose: A lightweight CalDAV and CardDAV server built on PHP and the sabre/dav library. Provides a clean web admin interface for managing users, calendars, and address books. Uses SQLite by default (MySQL/PostgreSQL supported) and runs on any PHP-capable host. Easy web-based setup wizard gets you running in minutes.
entries.pick: you want a lightweight CalDAV/CardDAV server with a user-friendly web admin panel for managing calendars and contacts, and you're comfortable running PHP.

alternatives.name: Radicale
alternatives.text: Baikal has a polished web UI for administration and uses a proper database. Radicale is even lighter, needs no database, and stores everything as flat files. Choose Baikal if you want a GUI for user management; Radicale if you want maximum simplicity and file-based storage.

alternatives.name: Cal.com
alternatives.text: Different tools. Baikal syncs calendar/contact data across devices via CalDAV/CardDAV. Cal.com is a scheduling platform for booking meetings. They can complement each other (Baikal for your private calendar, Cal.com for public booking pages).

alternatives.name: Twenty
alternatives.text: No overlap. Baikal is a calendar/contacts server; Twenty is a CRM for customer data and sales pipelines.

entries.name: Cal.com
prose: An open-source scheduling platform — the self-hosted Calendly alternative. Offers booking pages, team scheduling, round-robin assignment, calendar integrations (Google Calendar, Outlook, CalDAV), webhooks, workflows, and recurring events. White-label by design with full API access. The community edition (Cal.diy) is MIT-licensed and maintained independently for personal/non-production use.
entries.pick: you want a modern, full-featured scheduling and booking platform that replaces Calendly — letting others book meetings with you through customizable booking pages.

alternatives.name: Radicale
alternatives.text: Different purposes. Cal.com is for public-facing scheduling/booking; Radicale is for private CalDAV/CardDAV sync. Cal.com can connect to CalDAV servers (including Radicale) as a calendar source.

alternatives.name: Baikal
alternatives.text: Same distinction: Baikal syncs your calendar data, Cal.com presents booking pages to the world. They're complementary, not competing.

alternatives.name: Twenty
alternatives.text: Cal.com handles scheduling; Twenty handles CRM. They could integrate (book meetings with CRM contacts), but serve different needs. Cal.com if you need booking pages; Twenty if you need pipeline/contact management.

entries.name: Twenty
prose: A modern, open-source CRM built as an alternative to Salesforce. Developer-friendly with a clean UI, custom objects/fields, kanban pipelines, email integration, notes, tasks, and a GraphQL API. Designed for technical teams who want to own their CRM data and extend the platform like the rest of their stack. Supports custom workflows, views, and data models.
entries.pick: you want a modern, self-hosted CRM with a Notion-like UI that gives you full ownership of customer data — especially if you're a technical team wanting extensibility via API and custom objects.

alternatives.name: Radicale
alternatives.text: No overlap. Radicale is a calendar/contacts sync server; Twenty is a full CRM for managing customer relationships, deals, and pipelines.

alternatives.name: Baikal
alternatives.text: No overlap. Baikal serves CalDAV/CardDAV for calendar and contact sync; Twenty manages business relationships and sales processes. Twenty has its own contact management but it's CRM-focused, not CalDAV.

alternatives.name: Cal.com
alternatives.text: Complementary tools. Twenty tracks customer relationships and pipelines; Cal.com handles scheduling and booking. A team might use both — Twenty for the CRM, Cal.com to book calls with prospects.

categories.label: CMS & Blogs
categories.description: Content management systems, blogging platforms, and static site generators

entries.name: WordPress
prose: World's most popular CMS, powering ~40% of all websites. Full-featured content management with a massive ecosystem of themes and plugins. Supports everything from simple blogs to complex e-commerce sites. Requires PHP + MySQL/MariaDB.
entries.pick: you want the largest plugin/theme ecosystem, need non-technical editors to manage content, or are migrating an existing WordPress site to self-hosted.

alternatives.name: Ghost
alternatives.text: WordPress if you need plugin extensibility, e-commerce (WooCommerce), or complex multi-author workflows; Ghost if you want a clean, fast publishing experience without plugin sprawl.

alternatives.name: Strapi
alternatives.text: WordPress if you want a traditional CMS with built-in frontend and WYSIWYG; Strapi if you need a headless API-first CMS for custom frontends.

alternatives.name: Hugo
alternatives.text: WordPress if you need dynamic content, user accounts, comments, or non-technical editing; Hugo if you want maximum speed, zero runtime dependencies, and are comfortable with markdown + git workflows.

entries.name: Ghost

fields.Backup: Ghost CLI export (JSON) + `/content` dir + MySQL dump

prose: Modern publishing platform focused on professional blogging and newsletters. Built-in membership and subscription support (paid newsletters, gated content). Clean editor with markdown and card-based rich content. Requires Node.js + MySQL.
entries.pick: you want a polished publishing experience with native newsletter/membership features and don't need arbitrary plugin extensibility.

alternatives.name: WordPress
alternatives.text: Ghost if you want a focused, fast writing experience with native subscriptions; WordPress if you need unlimited extensibility via plugins or WooCommerce.

alternatives.name: Hugo
alternatives.text: Ghost if you want a web-based editor, memberships, and newsletters out of the box; Hugo if you want static output, git-based workflow, and zero runtime.

alternatives.name: Strapi
alternatives.text: Ghost if you want a complete publishing platform (editor + frontend + email); Strapi if you need a headless CMS to power a custom frontend via API.

entries.name: Hugo

fields.Deploy: binary, docker (build-time only; output is static HTML)
fields.Resource: light (~50MB build-time; output served by any web server)
fields.Auth: N/A (static site; add external auth if needed)

prose: Fastest static site generator. Builds thousands of pages in seconds from markdown files. Single Go binary, no runtime dependencies. Output is plain HTML/CSS/JS — deploy anywhere (Nginx, Caddy, S3, Cloudflare Pages). Huge theme ecosystem.
entries.pick: you want blazing-fast builds, git-based content workflow, zero server-side attack surface, and are comfortable writing in markdown.

alternatives.name: WordPress
alternatives.text: Hugo if you want maximum performance, security (no runtime), and git-managed content; WordPress if you need dynamic features, web-based editing, or non-technical authors.

alternatives.name: Ghost
alternatives.text: Hugo if you don't need memberships/newsletters and prefer a local dev workflow with instant builds; Ghost if you want a web-based editor and built-in subscription management.

alternatives.name: Strapi
alternatives.text: Hugo if your content is markdown in git and doesn't need an API; Strapi if you need structured content delivered via REST/GraphQL to multiple frontends.

entries.name: Strapi

fields.Auth: built-in RBAC, API tokens, SSO (Enterprise Edition)

prose: Leading open-source headless CMS. Define content types via UI or code, expose them through auto-generated REST and GraphQL APIs. Fully customizable admin panel. Powers decoupled frontends (Next.js, Nuxt, Gatsby, mobile apps). Supports SQLite, PostgreSQL, and MySQL.
entries.pick: you need a headless CMS with a visual content builder, REST/GraphQL APIs, and want to power custom frontends (React, Vue, mobile) with structured content.

alternatives.name: WordPress
alternatives.text: Strapi if you want API-first headless architecture for modern frontends; WordPress if you want a monolithic CMS with built-in rendering and massive plugin ecosystem.

alternatives.name: Ghost
alternatives.text: Strapi if you need fully custom content models and API delivery; Ghost if you want an opinionated publishing platform with built-in frontend and newsletters.

alternatives.name: Hugo
alternatives.text: Strapi if you need a web-based content editor, user roles, and API delivery to multiple clients; Hugo if your content lives in git and you just need static HTML output.

categories.label: Communication
categories.description: Chat, messaging, video conferencing, and team collaboration

entries.name: Matrix/Element
prose: Decentralized, end-to-end encrypted communication protocol with the Element client. Supports federation — your server talks to other Matrix servers across the internet. Offers rooms, spaces (room groups), DMs, file sharing, VoIP, and bridges to other platforms (Slack, Discord, IRC, Telegram).
entries.pick: you want decentralized, federated chat with strong encryption that you own entirely, or need to bridge multiple chat platforms into one interface.

alternatives.name: Rocket.Chat
alternatives.text: Matrix is a protocol (federate with anyone); Rocket.Chat is a monolithic app (richer out-of-box features, no federation). Matrix wins on sovereignty and interop; Rocket.Chat wins on ease of deployment and built-in features.

alternatives.name: Zulip
alternatives.text: Matrix focuses on real-time chat and encryption; Zulip focuses on threaded, async-friendly conversation. Pick Matrix for encrypted DMs and federation; Zulip for organized team discussions.

alternatives.name: Jitsi Meet
alternatives.text: Matrix handles text/VoIP; Jitsi handles video conferencing. Element can embed Jitsi for video calls.

entries.name: Rocket.Chat
prose: Full-featured Slack alternative with channels, DMs, threads, file sharing, video calls, and a marketplace of integrations. Supports omnichannel (live chat for websites), bots, and extensive admin controls. Mobile and desktop apps available.
entries.pick: you want a batteries-included Slack replacement with a familiar UI, rich integrations, and minimal setup time.

alternatives.name: Matrix/Element
alternatives.text: Rocket.Chat is simpler to deploy and has more built-in features (omnichannel, marketplace); Matrix offers federation and stronger E2EE. Pick Rocket.Chat for a team that just wants Slack-but-self-hosted; Matrix if you want decentralization.

alternatives.name: Zulip
alternatives.text: Rocket.Chat mimics Slack's real-time stream; Zulip enforces topic-based threading for every message. Pick Rocket.Chat for Slack muscle memory; Zulip for teams drowning in unread channels.

alternatives.name: Jitsi Meet
alternatives.text: Rocket.Chat includes basic video calling; Jitsi is purpose-built for large-scale video meetings. You can integrate Jitsi into Rocket.Chat for better video.

entries.name: Jitsi Meet
prose: Self-hosted video conferencing with no account required for guests. Supports screen sharing, recording (Jibri), live streaming, breakout rooms, polls, and end-to-end encryption. Works in-browser — no client install needed.
entries.pick: you want a privacy-respecting Zoom/Google Meet alternative where guests can join without creating accounts.

alternatives.name: Matrix/Element
alternatives.text: Jitsi is pure video conferencing; Matrix is persistent chat with optional VoIP. Use Jitsi for meetings, Matrix for ongoing conversation. Element can embed Jitsi as its video backend.

alternatives.name: Rocket.Chat
alternatives.text: Jitsi is dedicated video infrastructure; Rocket.Chat has basic video built in. Integrate Jitsi into Rocket.Chat for production-quality video.

alternatives.name: Zulip
alternatives.text: No overlap — Jitsi is video, Zulip is text. Zulip can link out to Jitsi for meetings.

entries.name: Zulip

fields.Resource: medium (~1GB with PostgreSQL + memcached + Redis + RabbitMQ)
fields.Auth: built-in, LDAP, SAML, OIDC, GitHub/Google OAuth
fields.Reverse proxy: ✓ (built-in nginx, or front with your own)

prose: Threaded team chat that combines the immediacy of real-time chat with the organization of email. Every message belongs to a stream (channel) and a topic (thread), making it easy to catch up on specific conversations without reading everything. Powerful search, markdown rendering, and integrations.
entries.pick: your team struggles with "too many unreads" in Slack-style tools, or you need async-friendly communication where discussions stay organized over days/weeks.

alternatives.name: Rocket.Chat
alternatives.text: Zulip enforces topics on every message, making catch-up trivial; Rocket.Chat is a closer Slack clone. Pick Zulip for async-heavy or distributed teams; Rocket.Chat for teams that prefer Slack's UX.

alternatives.name: Matrix/Element
alternatives.text: Zulip is a single-server team tool focused on threading; Matrix is a federated protocol focused on encryption and interop. Different purposes — Zulip for organized team comms, Matrix for sovereign encrypted messaging.

alternatives.name: Jitsi Meet
alternatives.text: No overlap — Zulip is text-based team chat, Jitsi is video. Zulip supports embedding Jitsi links for ad-hoc video calls.

categories.label: Containers & Orchestration
categories.description: Container management, orchestration, and self-hosting platforms

entries.name: Portainer
prose: Full-featured Docker and Kubernetes management UI. Provides container lifecycle management, stack deployment (compose), image management, network/volume configuration, registries, environment management, and role-based access control. Supports multi-node via Portainer Agent or Edge Agent for remote/edge environments.
entries.pick: you need a production-grade container management UI with RBAC, multi-environment support (Docker standalone, Swarm, Kubernetes), and team workflows.

alternatives.name: Coolify
alternatives.text: Portainer is a container management platform (operate what's running); Coolify is a deployment platform (push code, get a running app). Portainer for ops visibility; Coolify for developer PaaS workflows.

alternatives.name: Dockge
alternatives.text: Portainer covers the full Docker/K8s surface (containers, images, networks, volumes, registries); Dockge focuses purely on compose stack management with a cleaner UX for that one job.

alternatives.name: CasaOS
alternatives.text: Portainer is a professional container management tool; CasaOS is a consumer-friendly home-server OS. Portainer for power users managing infrastructure; CasaOS for non-technical users who want an app-store experience.

entries.name: Coolify

fields.Backup: built-in database/volume backups to S3-compatible storage

prose: Self-hostable PaaS alternative to Heroku, Vercel, and Netlify. Deploys apps from Git repos (any language/framework), supports Dockerfiles, docker-compose, and pre-built images. Includes automatic SSL, preview deployments, database provisioning (Postgres, MySQL, Redis, MongoDB), S3 backups, webhooks, and multi-server management.
entries.pick: you want a self-hosted Heroku/Vercel — push code to Git, get automatic builds, TLS certificates, preview deploys, and managed databases without touching compose files or reverse proxy config.

alternatives.name: Portainer
alternatives.text: Coolify is for deploying applications from source code (developer PaaS); Portainer is for managing existing containers and infrastructure (ops tool). Use Coolify to ship apps; use Portainer to inspect and manage them.

alternatives.name: Dockge
alternatives.text: Coolify handles the full deploy pipeline (git → build → deploy → TLS → monitoring); Dockge is a lightweight compose file manager. Coolify for teams shipping apps; Dockge for homelab users managing stacks.

alternatives.name: CasaOS
alternatives.text: Coolify is developer-oriented (git integration, CI/CD, multi-server); CasaOS is consumer-oriented (app store, file manager, simple UI). Coolify replaces your PaaS; CasaOS replaces your NAS OS.

entries.name: Dockge
prose: Compose stack manager from the creator of Uptime Kuma. Manages `docker-compose.yml` files directly on disk — no database, no abstraction layer. Features a real-time terminal, interactive compose editor, container status, and multi-agent support for managing stacks across multiple hosts.
entries.pick: you want a clean, focused UI for managing docker-compose stacks that keeps your compose files as plain files on disk — no vendor lock-in, no abstraction, git-friendly.

alternatives.name: Portainer
alternatives.text: Dockge is compose-only with a simpler UX and files-on-disk philosophy; Portainer covers the entire Docker/K8s surface but abstracts compose files into its own database. Dockge for compose purists; Portainer for full platform management.

alternatives.name: Coolify
alternatives.text: Dockge manages existing compose stacks; Coolify builds and deploys apps from source. Dockge for "I wrote my compose file, help me run it"; Coolify for "here's my Git repo, deploy it."

alternatives.name: CasaOS
alternatives.text: Dockge gives you direct compose file control with a lightweight UI; CasaOS hides Docker behind an app-store metaphor. Dockge for users who think in compose; CasaOS for users who think in apps.

entries.name: CasaOS

fields.Deploy: install script (bare metal on Debian/Ubuntu/RPi OS)
fields.Image: N/A (system-level install; apps run as Docker containers)
fields.Resource: medium (~512MB base; varies by apps installed)
fields.Backup: app data via UI; system snapshots recommended separately

prose: Home server operating system with a polished web UI and one-click app store. Installs on top of existing Linux and provides file management, Docker app deployment (via curated store or custom compose), storage management, and a desktop-like web interface. Built by IceWhale (ZimaBoard makers).
entries.pick: you want a friendly, consumer-grade home server experience — install apps from a store, manage files, and share storage without touching the terminal or writing YAML.

alternatives.name: Portainer
alternatives.text: CasaOS is a full home-server OS experience (files, storage, app store); Portainer is purely a container management tool. CasaOS for appliance-like simplicity; Portainer for Docker/K8s power users.

alternatives.name: Coolify
alternatives.text: CasaOS is for running pre-packaged self-hosted apps at home; Coolify is for deploying your own applications from source code. CasaOS replaces Synology/Unraid; Coolify replaces Heroku.

alternatives.name: Dockge
alternatives.text: CasaOS wraps Docker in an app-store UI with file/storage management; Dockge exposes raw compose files with a thin management layer. CasaOS for "I want a NAS with apps"; Dockge for "I want to manage my stacks."

entries.name: Homarr
prose: Feature-rich homelab dashboard with drag-and-drop layout, deep integrations with Sonarr/Radarr/qBittorrent/Docker, and a widget ecosystem. Supports multiple boards, user permissions, and real-time service status.
entries.pick: you want a polished, interactive dashboard with live service integrations, drag-and-drop editing, and built-in multi-user auth.

alternatives.name: Homepage
alternatives.text: Homarr is more interactive with drag-and-drop and deeper media-stack integrations; Homepage is faster to configure via YAML and lighter on resources.

alternatives.name: Dashy
alternatives.text: Homarr is more opinionated with a modern UI and built-in integrations; Dashy offers more raw customization (themes, layouts, widgets) via config file.

alternatives.name: Homer

alternatives.name: Glance

entries.pick: you want a config-as-code dashboard that auto-discovers Docker/Kubernetes services and displays live stats with minimal resource use.

alternatives.name: Homarr

alternatives.name: Dashy

alternatives.name: Homer

alternatives.name: Glance

entries.name: Dashy

entries.pick: you want maximum visual and layout control — multiple themes, custom CSS, workspace-style views, and a massive icon library.

alternatives.name: Homarr

alternatives.name: Homepage

alternatives.name: Homer

alternatives.name: Glance
alternatives.text: Dashy is a full-featured dashboard builder; Glance is a minimalist single-column feed page.

entries.name: Homer
prose: Simple static homepage generator configured via a single YAML file. Supports service grouping, custom icons, search, themes, and optional health checks. Serves as plain HTML/JS with no backend.
entries.pick: you want the lightest possible homepage — a static links page with grouping and search, no database, no API calls, no dependencies.

alternatives.name: Homarr
alternatives.text: Homer is a static links page; Homarr is a full interactive dashboard. Homer when you just need bookmarks; Homarr when you want live widgets.

alternatives.name: Homepage
alternatives.text: Homer is static and simple; Homepage queries service APIs for live data. Homer for pure speed; Homepage for real-time info.

alternatives.name: Dashy

alternatives.name: Glance

entries.name: Glance
prose: Lightweight feed dashboard written in Go. Displays RSS feeds, weather, bookmarks, Hacker News, Reddit, calendar, Twitch, GitHub releases, and service monitors in a clean column layout. Single binary, fast startup, minimal resource use.
entries.pick: you want a personal startpage that aggregates feeds, weather, and bookmarks in a clean layout without the overhead of a full dashboard.

categories.label: Databases & Management
categories.description: Database servers, management tools, and admin interfaces

entries.name: PostgreSQL

fields.Reverse proxy: N/A (TCP 5432; use PgBouncer or stunnel for TLS)
fields.Backup: `pg_dump` / `pg_basebackup` / WAL archiving / restic on data dir

prose: The most advanced open-source relational database. Full SQL compliance, ACID transactions, JSONB, full-text search, extensions (PostGIS, pgvector, TimescaleDB), logical replication, and CTEs. The default choice for application backends.
entries.pick: you want a battle-tested relational database with rich extension ecosystem, advanced SQL features, and long-term reliability.

alternatives.name: MariaDB
alternatives.text: PostgreSQL has stronger standards compliance, better JSONB support, and a richer extension ecosystem. MariaDB is lighter on resources and a drop-in MySQL replacement.

alternatives.name: Redis / Valkey
alternatives.text: Different layer. PostgreSQL is durable disk-based storage; Redis is an in-memory cache/broker. Often used together.

entries.name: MariaDB

fields.Reverse proxy: N/A (TCP 3306; use ProxySQL or stunnel for TLS)

prose: Community-developed fork of MySQL with full wire-protocol compatibility. Adds Aria storage engine, ColumnStore for analytics, and improved replication. Most MySQL-targeting apps (WordPress, Nextcloud, Gitea) work unmodified.
entries.pick: you need MySQL compatibility for existing apps, prefer a community-governed fork, or want a lighter relational DB for standard CRUD workloads.

alternatives.name: PostgreSQL
alternatives.text: MariaDB is simpler to operate for MySQL-ecosystem apps; PostgreSQL is more capable for complex queries, JSONB, and extensions.

alternatives.name: Adminer
alternatives.text: MariaDB is the database engine; Adminer is a web UI to manage it.

entries.name: Redis / Valkey

fields.Resource: light (~50MB base, grows with dataset in RAM)
fields.Reverse proxy: N/A (TCP 6379; TLS built-in since Redis 6 / Valkey)

prose: In-memory data structure store used as cache, message broker, session store, and rate limiter. Sub-millisecond latency. Valkey is the community fork after Redis changed to a non-open-source license in 2024 — API-compatible, same commands and clients.
entries.pick: you need a fast cache layer, session store, job queue (Sidekiq/BullMQ), or pub/sub broker alongside your primary database.

alternatives.name: PostgreSQL / MariaDB
alternatives.text: Redis/Valkey is in-memory and ephemeral by default; relational DBs are durable primary storage. Use them together: DB for truth, Redis for speed.

alternatives.name: Adminer
alternatives.text: No overlap; Adminer doesn't manage Redis. Use `redis-cli` or RedisInsight for Redis admin.

entries.name: Adminer

fields.Config: `plugins/` directory, CSS themes, env vars for defaults
fields.Backup: stateless (no local data to back up)

prose: Single-file PHP database admin interface supporting PostgreSQL, MySQL/MariaDB, SQLite, MS SQL, Oracle, and MongoDB. Lighter and faster than phpMyAdmin with multi-driver support in one tool.
entries.pick: you want a minimal, zero-dependency web UI to browse and manage multiple database engines from one interface.

alternatives.name: phpMyAdmin
alternatives.text: Adminer is a single file, supports multiple DB engines, and has a cleaner UI. phpMyAdmin is MySQL-only and heavier.

alternatives.name: pgAdmin
alternatives.text: Adminer is multi-database and lightweight; pgAdmin is PostgreSQL-specific with richer PG tooling (explain plans, server groups).

categories.label: Development
categories.description: Git forges, CI/CD, code review, and developer tooling

entries.name: Forgejo
prose: Lightweight Git forge — code hosting, pull requests, CI (Forgejo Actions), packages. Community-governed fork of Gitea.
entries.pick: you want community governance, low resource usage, and GitHub Actions-compatible CI without the corporate overhead.

alternatives.name: Gitea
alternatives.text: Forgejo if you want community governance; Gitea if you want the larger plugin ecosystem.

alternatives.name: GitLab CE
alternatives.text: Forgejo if you want lightweight; GitLab if you need built-in CI/CD + container registry at scale (and can spare 4GB RAM).

entries.name: Gitea
prose: Lightweight Git forge with a large plugin/integration ecosystem. Originally inspired by Gogs.
entries.pick: you want a mature, lightweight forge with broad community integrations and permissive licensing.

alternatives.name: Forgejo
alternatives.text: Gitea if you want commercial backing and wider integrations; Forgejo if you prefer community governance.

alternatives.name: GitLab CE
alternatives.text: Same tradeoff as Forgejo: lightweight vs full-fat CI/CD platform.

entries.name: GitLab CE
prose: Full DevOps platform — Git hosting, CI/CD pipelines, container registry, issue tracking, wiki, pages, and more. All-in-one but resource-hungry.
entries.pick: you want a single platform for everything from code to deployment and can afford the RAM.

alternatives.name: Forgejo/Gitea
alternatives.text: GitLab if you need built-in CI, registry, and project management in one box; Forgejo/Gitea if you want lightweight and composable.

categories.label: Documents & Knowledge
categories.description: Document management, OCR, PDF tools, and knowledge bases

entries.name: Paperless-ngx
prose: Document management system that ingests paper documents (via scanner or file upload), runs OCR with Tesseract, and indexes everything for full-text search. Automatic tagging, correspondent detection, and date parsing. Supports consumption from directories, email, and mobile apps.
entries.pick: you want to go paperless — scan/photograph documents and have them automatically OCR'd, tagged, searchable, and archived with minimal manual effort.

alternatives.name: Stirling-PDF
alternatives.text: Paperless-ngx is a full document management system (ingest, OCR, archive, search); Stirling-PDF is a stateless toolkit for manipulating existing PDFs. They complement rather than compete.

alternatives.name: BookStack
alternatives.text: Paperless-ngx manages scanned/uploaded documents (invoices, receipts, letters); BookStack is for writing and organizing knowledge. Different use cases.

alternatives.name: Outline
alternatives.text: Paperless-ngx archives existing documents; Outline is for creating new collaborative documents. Use both together.

entries.name: Stirling-PDF

fields.Backup: stateless — only persist `/configs` if auth is enabled

prose: Self-hosted PDF manipulation toolkit. Merge, split, rotate, compress, convert, watermark, sign, OCR, and dozens more operations via a clean web UI. Entirely stateless — files are processed and returned, never stored.
entries.pick: you need an all-in-one PDF Swiss army knife without uploading sensitive documents to cloud services like ILovePDF or Adobe.

alternatives.name: Paperless-ngx
alternatives.text: Stirling-PDF is a stateless tool for one-off PDF operations; Paperless-ngx stores and manages your document archive long-term. Use Stirling-PDF to prep files before feeding them to Paperless-ngx.

alternatives.name: BookStack
alternatives.text: No overlap. Stirling-PDF manipulates PDF files; BookStack is a wiki platform.

entries.name: BookStack
prose: Wiki and documentation platform organized around a books/chapters/pages hierarchy. WYSIWYG and Markdown editors, diagrams (draw.io integration), full-text search, role-based permissions, revision history, and PDF/HTML export.
entries.pick: you want a structured wiki for documentation, runbooks, or knowledge that benefits from a hierarchical book/chapter/page model and a straightforward UI.

alternatives.name: Outline
alternatives.text: BookStack if you prefer a rigid hierarchy (books → chapters → pages) and simpler self-hosting; Outline if you want a flatter structure, real-time collaboration, and a Notion-like feel.

alternatives.name: Paperless-ngx
alternatives.text: BookStack is for authored documentation; Paperless-ngx is for archived scanned documents. Different purposes, often used side by side.

entries.name: Outline

fields.Resource: medium (~300MB; requires PostgreSQL + Redis + S3-compatible storage)
fields.License: BSL-1.1 (source-available, converts to Apache-2.0 after 4 years)

prose: Modern, fast wiki designed for teams. Real-time collaborative editing, slash commands, Markdown-native, nested collections, public sharing, API-first. Feels like Notion but self-hosted.
entries.pick: you want a modern, Notion-like knowledge base with real-time collaboration and you already have an OIDC provider (Authentik, Keycloak, etc.) for auth.

alternatives.name: BookStack
alternatives.text: Outline if you want real-time collab, a Notion-like UX, and a flat/flexible structure; BookStack if you prefer strict hierarchy and simpler deployment (no mandatory OIDC).

alternatives.name: Paperless-ngx
alternatives.text: Outline is for writing and collaborating on living documents; Paperless-ngx is for archiving scanned/uploaded static documents.

categories.label: E-commerce
categories.description: Online stores, payment processing, and shop management

entries.name: WooCommerce
prose: The dominant open-source e-commerce platform, built as a WordPress plugin. Inherits the entire WordPress ecosystem — themes, plugins, page builders, SEO tools. Handles physical and digital products, variable products, shipping zones, tax rules, coupons, and dozens of payment gateways. REST API available for headless use but not its primary design.
entries.pick: you already run WordPress, want the largest plugin/theme ecosystem, or need a traditional server-rendered storefront with minimal custom development.

alternatives.name: Saleor
alternatives.text: WooCommerce is monolithic (server-rendered pages, PHP); Saleor is headless-first (GraphQL API, bring your own frontend). WooCommerce has vastly more plugins but Saleor gives full frontend freedom.

alternatives.name: Medusa
alternatives.text: WooCommerce is a WordPress plugin with a bundled storefront; Medusa is a standalone headless engine. WooCommerce is easier to launch without a developer; Medusa is easier to customize programmatically.

alternatives.name: PrestaShop
alternatives.text: Both are traditional full-stack platforms. WooCommerce rides on WordPress (content + commerce together); PrestaShop is purpose-built for commerce with deeper built-in merchandising (product combinations, stock management, multi-store).

entries.name: Saleor
prose: Python/Django headless commerce engine exposing a comprehensive GraphQL API. Designed for custom storefronts (Next.js, Gatsby, mobile apps). Supports multi-channel selling, multi-currency, multi-warehouse, gift cards, vouchers, draft orders, and a plugin/webhook system for extensibility. Ships with a React-based admin dashboard.
entries.pick: you want a Python-native headless commerce backend with GraphQL, multi-channel support, and plan to build a custom frontend.

alternatives.name: Medusa
alternatives.text: Both are headless-first. Saleor uses Python/Django + GraphQL; Medusa uses Node.js + REST (GraphQL via plugin). Saleor has more built-in enterprise features (multi-warehouse, multi-channel); Medusa is more modular and easier to extend with custom logic.

alternatives.name: WooCommerce
alternatives.text: Saleor is headless (API-only, bring your own frontend); WooCommerce bundles a storefront. Saleor suits custom builds; WooCommerce suits quick launches with off-the-shelf themes.

alternatives.name: PrestaShop
alternatives.text: Saleor is headless and developer-oriented (GraphQL, custom frontend); PrestaShop is a full-stack platform with a built-in storefront and admin. PrestaShop is faster to launch without custom development; Saleor gives total frontend control.

entries.name: Medusa
prose: Node.js headless commerce engine with a modular architecture. Exposes REST APIs (and GraphQL via plugin) for storefronts. Extensible through services, subscribers, and custom endpoints. Supports regions, multi-currency, tax-inclusive pricing, gift cards, discounts, swaps, returns, and order editing. Ships with a React admin dashboard and a Next.js starter storefront.
entries.pick: you want a JavaScript/TypeScript headless commerce backend that's highly modular, MIT-licensed, and easy to extend with custom business logic.

alternatives.name: Saleor
alternatives.text: Medusa is Node.js/TypeScript with REST-first APIs and a plug-in-based architecture; Saleor is Python/Django with GraphQL. Medusa is lighter and more modular; Saleor has more built-in enterprise features out of the box.

alternatives.name: WooCommerce
alternatives.text: Medusa is a headless engine (you build or pick a frontend); WooCommerce is a full-stack WordPress plugin. Medusa favors developer-driven customization; WooCommerce favors no-code/low-code store setup.

alternatives.name: PrestaShop
alternatives.text: Medusa is headless (API + custom frontend); PrestaShop is full-stack (admin + storefront included). Medusa suits teams building a unique checkout/storefront experience; PrestaShop suits merchants who want a ready-to-use shop.

entries.name: PrestaShop
prose: Full-featured e-commerce platform built in PHP/Symfony. Ships with a complete storefront, back office, and module marketplace. Handles product combinations (size/color), advanced stock management, multi-store, multi-language, carrier configuration, invoice generation, and customer groups. Large European user base with strong localization support.
entries.pick: you want a standalone, full-stack e-commerce platform with deep built-in merchandising features, multi-store support, and a module marketplace — without depending on WordPress.

alternatives.name: WooCommerce
alternatives.text: Both are PHP full-stack platforms. PrestaShop is purpose-built for commerce (better native stock management, product combinations, multi-store); WooCommerce rides on WordPress (better for content-heavy sites, larger ecosystem).

alternatives.name: Saleor
alternatives.text: PrestaShop is a complete platform (storefront + admin included); Saleor is headless (API-only, build your own frontend). PrestaShop is faster to launch; Saleor offers more frontend flexibility.

alternatives.name: Medusa
alternatives.text: PrestaShop includes everything out of the box (themes, checkout, admin); Medusa is a backend engine requiring a custom frontend. PrestaShop suits merchants; Medusa suits developers building bespoke experiences.

categories.label: Email
categories.description: Complete mail servers, webmail clients, and email infrastructure

entries.name: Stalwart Mail Server

fields.Resource: low–medium (~256MB; single binary, no external DB required)
fields.Config: TOML config file + web admin UI
fields.Backup: built-in data export, or snapshot the data directory

prose: All-in-one mail server written in Rust supporting JMAP, IMAP4, POP3, and SMTP. Ships as a single binary with built-in spam filtering (sieve), full-text search, web admin panel, and webmail. No external database required — uses an embedded RocksDB/SQLite store by default, but can connect to PostgreSQL/MySQL. Handles DKIM signing, DMARC, SPF, ARC, MTA-STS, and DANE out of the box.
entries.pick: you want a modern, memory-efficient, all-in-one mail server with minimal moving parts — especially if JMAP support matters to you or you prefer a single-binary deployment over a multi-container stack.

alternatives.name: docker-mailserver
alternatives.text: Stalwart is a single Rust binary with built-in everything (spam filter, full-text search, webmail); docker-mailserver assembles battle-tested components (Postfix, Dovecot, Rspamd) into one container. Pick Stalwart for simplicity and modern protocols (JMAP); docker-mailserver for the proven Postfix/Dovecot ecosystem and extensive community docs.

alternatives.name: Mailu
alternatives.text: Both are all-in-one solutions, but Stalwart is a single process while Mailu is a multi-container suite with its own webmail and admin UI. Pick Stalwart for lower resource use and JMAP; Mailu for a more batteries-included Docker experience with built-in antivirus and webmail choices.

alternatives.name: Roundcube
alternatives.text: No overlap — Stalwart is a mail server (MTA + MDA); Roundcube is a webmail client. Stalwart includes its own webmail, but you can point Roundcube at Stalwart's IMAP if you prefer it.

entries.name: docker-mailserver

fields.Resource: medium (~512MB; Postfix + Dovecot + Rspamd + ClamAV optional)
fields.Backup: mail data (`/var/mail`) + config directory + optional DKIM keys

prose: Production-ready mail server built on Postfix (SMTP) and Dovecot (IMAP/POP3) packed into a single Docker container. Includes Rspamd for spam filtering, optional ClamAV for antivirus, Fail2Ban for brute-force protection, and Let's Encrypt integration. Configuration is file-based (no database), managed through a `setup.sh` helper or by editing flat files directly.
entries.pick: you want a proven, well-documented Postfix/Dovecot stack that runs in a single container with minimal fuss — particularly if your team already understands traditional mail server components.

alternatives.name: Stalwart
alternatives.text: docker-mailserver uses established, battle-hardened components (Postfix/Dovecot) with decades of community knowledge; Stalwart is newer but simpler (single binary, built-in everything). Pick docker-mailserver for production confidence and ecosystem familiarity; Stalwart for lower overhead and modern protocols.

alternatives.name: Mailu
alternatives.text: Both use Postfix/Dovecot under the hood, but docker-mailserver is a single container configured via flat files, while Mailu is a multi-container suite with a web admin UI and integrated webmail. Pick docker-mailserver for tighter control and fewer moving parts; Mailu for a more GUI-friendly experience.

alternatives.name: Roundcube
alternatives.text: No overlap — docker-mailserver is the mail server (MTA + MDA); Roundcube provides a web UI for reading/sending. Pair them together for a complete self-hosted email stack.

entries.name: Mailu

fields.Resource: medium (~512MB base; more with antivirus enabled)
fields.Reverse proxy: built-in nginx front (`mailu/front`); can sit behind external proxy
fields.Backup: mail data + PostgreSQL/SQLite admin DB + DKIM keys

prose: Simple, full-featured Docker mail suite that bundles Postfix, Dovecot, Rspamd, an admin web UI, and a choice of webmail (Roundcube or SnappyMail) into a coordinated Compose stack. Includes automatic TLS, DKIM/DMARC/SPF, rate limiting, quotas, aliases, and domain management — all configurable through the admin panel. Ships a setup wizard that generates your Compose file.
entries.pick: you want an opinionated, GUI-managed mail suite that handles everything (server + webmail + admin + antispam) in one Compose stack with minimal manual configuration.

alternatives.name: docker-mailserver
alternatives.text: Mailu adds a web admin UI, integrated webmail, and multi-container architecture; docker-mailserver is a leaner single container managed via CLI/flat files. Pick Mailu for a friendlier admin experience; docker-mailserver for simplicity and direct control.

alternatives.name: Stalwart
alternatives.text: Mailu is a traditional Postfix/Dovecot stack wrapped in Docker with admin UI; Stalwart is a modern single-binary rewrite in Rust. Pick Mailu for proven components and built-in webmail choice; Stalwart for lower resource use, JMAP, and fewer containers.

alternatives.name: Roundcube
alternatives.text: Mailu includes Roundcube (or SnappyMail) as its webmail component. If you run Mailu, you already have webmail — no need to deploy Roundcube separately.

entries.name: Roundcube

fields.Auth: IMAP passthrough (login = IMAP credentials), OAuth2, LDAP address book

prose: Mature, widely-deployed webmail client with a clean interface for reading, composing, and organizing email. Supports drag-and-drop, address books, identities, filters (ManageSieve), folder management, and a plugin ecosystem for calendars, 2FA, and skins. Connects to any IMAP server — it's a frontend only, not a mail server.
entries.pick: you already have a mail server (Stalwart, docker-mailserver, or any IMAP server) and want a polished, reliable webmail UI without the bloat of a full groupware suite.

alternatives.name: Stalwart
alternatives.text: Roundcube is a webmail client; Stalwart is a mail server that includes its own webmail. Use Roundcube if you prefer its UI or plugin ecosystem over Stalwart's built-in webmail.

alternatives.name: docker-mailserver
alternatives.text: Complementary — docker-mailserver handles SMTP/IMAP; Roundcube provides the web UI on top. Deploy both for a complete stack.

alternatives.name: Mailu
alternatives.text: Mailu bundles Roundcube (or SnappyMail) as its webmail layer. If you're not using Mailu but have another mail server, deploy Roundcube standalone for webmail access.

categories.label: Feeds & Bookmarks
categories.description: RSS readers, feed aggregators, bookmark managers, and read-later tools

entries.name: FreshRSS
prose: Full-featured, self-hosted RSS aggregator supporting multiple users, categories, labels, search, and an extension system. Compatible with Google Reader API and Fever API for third-party mobile clients. Supports WebSub for real-time push notifications from compatible feeds.
entries.pick: you want a batteries-included RSS reader with multi-user support, extension ecosystem, and broad mobile client compatibility.

alternatives.name: Miniflux
alternatives.text: FreshRSS if you want extensions, theming, and Google Reader API; Miniflux if you want minimal footprint, native Fever/GReader API without extensions, and a cleaner reading UI.

alternatives.name: Wallabag
alternatives.text: FreshRSS for feed aggregation and subscription management; Wallabag for saving individual articles and reading them later offline.

entries.name: Miniflux

fields.Resource: very light (~30MB idle, single Go binary)

prose: Minimalist, opinionated feed reader written in Go. Single binary, PostgreSQL-backed, fast and clean. Built-in Fever and Google Reader API support for mobile clients. Focuses on reading experience with no bloat — no extensions, no themes, just feeds.
entries.pick: you want the leanest RSS reader with excellent performance, prefer configuration via env vars, and don't need extensions or theming.

alternatives.name: FreshRSS
alternatives.text: Miniflux if you value minimalism, speed, and a single-binary deployment; FreshRSS if you want extensions, multiple database backends, and more customization.

alternatives.name: Wallabag
alternatives.text: Miniflux for subscribing to and reading feeds in real-time; Wallabag for archiving and reading specific articles later.

entries.name: Linkwarden
prose: Collaborative bookmark and archive manager. Saves bookmarks with full-page screenshots and PDF/HTML archives. Supports collections, tags, sharing, and collaboration. Browser extensions for quick saving. Automatically preserves pages so content isn't lost when sites go down.
entries.pick: you want a modern bookmark manager with automatic page archiving, collaboration features, and a polished UI for organizing web links.

alternatives.name: Wallabag
alternatives.text: Linkwarden for bookmark organization, collections, collaboration, and full-page archiving; Wallabag for distraction-free article reading and offline text extraction.

alternatives.name: FreshRSS
alternatives.text: Linkwarden for saving individual pages you discover; FreshRSS for subscribing to sites and reading new content as it appears.

entries.name: Wallabag
prose: Self-hosted read-later and article archiver (Pocket/Instapaper alternative). Extracts article text from web pages, strips clutter, and stores clean readable versions. Supports tagging, annotations, full-text search, and export to ePub/PDF. Mobile apps and browser extensions available.
entries.pick: you want a Pocket replacement — save articles, read distraction-free later (including offline), and annotate/tag for future reference.

alternatives.name: Linkwarden
alternatives.text: Wallabag for clean article extraction and distraction-free reading; Linkwarden for full-page archiving, screenshots, and bookmark organization with collaboration.

alternatives.name: FreshRSS
alternatives.text: Wallabag for saving and reading individual articles on your own schedule; FreshRSS for subscribing to feeds and staying current with new posts.

alternatives.name: Miniflux
alternatives.text: Wallabag for read-later workflow and article archiving; Miniflux for real-time feed consumption.

categories.label: File Sync & Storage
categories.description: File synchronization, cloud storage, object storage, and file sharing

entries.name: Nextcloud
prose: Full self-hosted collaboration platform — file sync, calendar, contacts, mail, office docs, video calls, and 400+ apps. The "Swiss army knife" of self-hosting. Desktop and mobile sync clients available.
entries.pick: you want a single platform replacing Google Workspace / Microsoft 365 — files, calendar, contacts, and collaboration in one place.

alternatives.name: Syncthing
alternatives.text: Nextcloud is a full platform with web UI, sharing links, and apps; Syncthing is pure P2P file sync with no server or web sharing.

alternatives.name: Seafile
alternatives.text: Nextcloud has far more features but Seafile is significantly faster at raw file sync and uses fewer resources.

alternatives.name: MinIO
alternatives.text: Different use cases. Nextcloud is user-facing file management; MinIO is S3-compatible object storage for applications and backups.

entries.name: Syncthing

fields.Reverse proxy: ✓ (web UI only; sync uses BEP protocol)
fields.Backup: data is distributed by design; back up `~/.config/syncthing` for config

prose: Decentralized peer-to-peer file synchronization. No central server needed — devices sync directly (or via relay). Encrypted in transit, open protocol, works across Linux/Windows/macOS/Android.
entries.pick: you want zero-server file sync between your own devices with no cloud dependency — true P2P with no account or subscription.

alternatives.name: Nextcloud
alternatives.text: Syncthing has no web UI for file browsing or sharing links; it purely mirrors folders between devices. Nextcloud provides a full web interface and collaboration features.

alternatives.name: Seafile
alternatives.text: Syncthing is serverless P2P; Seafile is client-server with a central store, better for teams needing a canonical copy.

alternatives.name: MinIO
alternatives.text: Completely different. Syncthing syncs personal files between devices; MinIO serves objects via S3 API for applications.

entries.name: Seafile
prose: High-performance file sync and share platform. Uses content-addressed block-level deduplication for fast delta sync. Web UI, desktop clients, mobile apps. Markdown editing, file locking, versioning, and library encryption built-in.
entries.pick: you want fast, reliable file sync that handles large files and many small files better than Nextcloud — with fewer bells and whistles but solid core performance.

alternatives.name: Nextcloud
alternatives.text: Seafile is faster at sync (block-level dedup) and lighter on resources, but lacks Nextcloud's app ecosystem (calendar, contacts, mail, office).

alternatives.name: Syncthing
alternatives.text: Seafile provides a central server with web UI, sharing links, and team libraries; Syncthing is pure device-to-device with no central authority.

alternatives.name: MinIO
alternatives.text: Seafile is user-facing file management with sync clients; MinIO is S3 API infrastructure for apps and backups.

entries.name: MinIO

fields.Backup: replicate to another MinIO instance or use `mc mirror`

prose: S3-compatible object storage server. Drop-in replacement for Amazon S3 in self-hosted environments. Supports erasure coding, bucket versioning, lifecycle policies, event notifications, and multi-site replication.
entries.pick: you need S3-compatible object storage for application backends, backup targets (restic, Velero), Docker registries, or any tool that speaks S3 protocol.

alternatives.name: Nextcloud
alternatives.text: MinIO is infrastructure (S3 API for apps); Nextcloud is end-user file management. MinIO can back Nextcloud as its object storage layer.

alternatives.name: Syncthing
alternatives.text: No overlap. MinIO serves objects to applications; Syncthing syncs personal files between devices.

alternatives.name: Seafile
alternatives.text: MinIO is an object store accessed via S3 API; Seafile is a user-facing file sync platform with desktop clients and web UI.

categories.label: Finance
categories.description: Personal finance, budgeting, expense tracking, and invoicing

entries.name: Actual Budget
prose: Zero-sum (envelope) budgeting app inspired by YNAB. Local-first architecture means the UI runs entirely in-browser with a sync server for multi-device access. Import via OFX/QFX/CSV, bank-sync via GoCardless/SimpleFIN, and rule-based auto-categorization.
entries.pick: you want YNAB-style envelope budgeting without the subscription, with fast offline-capable UI and optional bank sync.

alternatives.name: Firefly III
alternatives.text: Actual is laser-focused on budgeting (give every dollar a job); Firefly III is a full double-entry bookkeeping system with reports, recurring transactions, and multi-currency.

alternatives.name: Ghostfolio
alternatives.text: Different domains. Actual tracks day-to-day spending and budgets; Ghostfolio tracks investment portfolios and market performance.

entries.name: Firefly III
prose: Full-featured personal finance manager with double-entry bookkeeping. Tracks transactions, budgets, categories, piggy banks, recurring transactions, and multi-currency accounts. Rich reporting with charts, rule engine for auto-categorization, and a REST API.
entries.pick: you want comprehensive financial tracking across multiple accounts with double-entry accuracy, detailed reports, and automation rules.

alternatives.name: Actual Budget
alternatives.text: Firefly III is a full accounting system (transactions, reports, reconciliation); Actual is purpose-built for envelope budgeting with a simpler, faster UI.

alternatives.name: Ghostfolio
alternatives.text: Firefly III tracks cash flow and day-to-day finances; Ghostfolio is specifically for investment portfolio tracking with market data integration.

entries.name: Ghostfolio
prose: Investment portfolio tracker with real-time market data. Supports stocks, ETFs, crypto, commodities, and precious metals. Provides portfolio allocation, performance charts, dividend tracking, and a Fear & Greed index. Multi-account, multi-currency with automatic exchange-rate conversion.
entries.pick: you want a privacy-first portfolio tracker to visualize holdings, performance, and allocation across brokers — without giving your data to Mint or Yahoo Finance.

alternatives.name: Actual Budget
alternatives.text: Different domains. Ghostfolio tracks investments and net worth from securities; Actual tracks day-to-day cash budgeting.

alternatives.name: Firefly III
alternatives.text: Ghostfolio specializes in investment tracking with live market data; Firefly III handles cash-flow bookkeeping. Pair them for full visibility (daily spending + portfolio).

categories.label: Games & Game Servers
categories.description: Game servers, game management panels, and multiplayer hosting

entries.name: Pelican Panel

fields.Resource: medium (~512MB panel + Wings daemon per node)

prose: Community-driven successor to Pterodactyl Panel. Web-based game server management with full Docker isolation — each game server runs in its own container with dedicated resources. Supports hundreds of games via "eggs" (server templates). Two components: Panel (web UI, API, database) and Wings (daemon that provisions and manages containers on each node).
entries.pick: you want a polished web UI to manage multiple game servers across multiple machines, with per-user permissions, Docker isolation, and a large ecosystem of community eggs.

alternatives.name: Crafty Controller
alternatives.text: Pelican for multi-game, multi-node hosting with Docker isolation and user management; Crafty if you only need Minecraft and want a simpler single-node setup.

alternatives.name: LinuxGSM
alternatives.text: Pelican if you want a web UI, user accounts, and Docker isolation; LinuxGSM if you prefer CLI-only, no overhead, and direct access to game server files.

entries.name: Crafty Controller
prose: Minecraft-focused server management panel. Supports Java and Bedrock editions. Web UI for creating servers, managing players, running commands, editing files, and scheduling backups. Built in Python, lightweight, and designed for single-node deployments.
entries.pick: you only run Minecraft servers (Java + Bedrock) and want a dedicated, lightweight panel with built-in backup scheduling and a file manager.

alternatives.name: Pelican Panel
alternatives.text: Crafty if Minecraft is all you need and you want simplicity; Pelican if you host multiple game types or need multi-node orchestration.

alternatives.name: LinuxGSM
alternatives.text: Crafty if you want a Minecraft-specific web UI with backup scheduling; LinuxGSM if you prefer CLI management and support for many game types beyond Minecraft.

entries.name: Sunshine

fields.Deploy: binary, package (deb, rpm, flatpak, exe, dmg)
fields.Image: n/a (runs as system service, not containerized)
fields.Resource: light (~100MB idle, GPU required for encoding)
fields.Auth: PIN pairing (Moonlight client pairs with host)

prose: Self-hosted game streaming host for Moonlight clients. Low-latency remote desktop and game streaming with hardware encoding support for AMD, Intel, and Nvidia GPUs. Software encoding fallback available. Replaces Nvidia GameStream (discontinued). Connect from any Moonlight client on PC, Mac, Android, iOS, or TV.
entries.pick: you want to stream games or your desktop from a host machine to other devices with minimal latency, especially as a replacement for Nvidia GameStream.

alternatives.name: Pelican Panel
alternatives.text: entirely different use case. Sunshine streams games to remote displays; Pelican manages dedicated game server processes.

alternatives.name: LinuxGSM
alternatives.text: Sunshine is for playing games remotely on your own hardware; LinuxGSM is for hosting multiplayer dedicated servers for others to connect to.

entries.name: LinuxGSM

fields.Reverse proxy: not applicable (game traffic is direct UDP/TCP)
fields.Config: cfg files per game server instance

prose: Command-line tool for quick deployment and management of 120+ Linux dedicated game servers. Handles installation, updates, monitoring, backups, and alerts via simple commands (`./csgoserver start`, `./csgoserver update`). No web UI — designed for admins comfortable with the terminal.
entries.pick: you want the fastest path to a running game server with minimal overhead, prefer CLI workflows, and don't need a web UI or multi-user access control.

alternatives.name: Pelican Panel
alternatives.text: LinuxGSM if you want zero overhead and direct file access; Pelican if you need a web UI, user permissions, and Docker isolation.

alternatives.name: Crafty Controller
alternatives.text: LinuxGSM if you want broad game support (120+ games) via CLI; Crafty if you specifically want a Minecraft web panel with GUI management.

categories.label: Home Automation
categories.description: Smart home platforms, IoT management, and device control

entries.name: Home Assistant

fields.Auth: built-in (user accounts), OIDC via auth proxy

prose: The most comprehensive open-source home automation platform. Integrates with 2000+ devices and services out of the box — Zigbee, Z-Wave, MQTT, Wi-Fi devices, cloud APIs, media players, climate systems, and more. Automations can be built in the UI or in YAML. Add-ons ecosystem provides Zigbee2MQTT, MQTT brokers, voice assistants, and databases as managed containers.
entries.pick: you want the widest device support, an active community, frequent updates, and a polished mobile app — the "just works" choice for most self-hosters.

alternatives.name: openHAB
alternatives.text: Home Assistant has broader integrations, faster release cadence, and a larger community. openHAB is more modular and better suited to complex rule engines or Java-friendly teams.

alternatives.name: Node-RED
alternatives.text: Home Assistant is the central hub (state, UI, device management); Node-RED is a flow-based programming tool you wire alongside it for complex logic or API orchestration.

entries.name: openHAB
prose: Vendor-agnostic home automation platform built on Java/OSGi. Strong separation between "things" (devices), "items" (state), and "rules" (logic). Supports 400+ bindings for protocols like KNX, EnOcean, Modbus, MQTT, Zigbee, and Z-Wave. Rule engine supports Blockly, JavaScript, and Jython.
entries.pick: you want explicit abstraction layers between physical devices and automation logic, need KNX or industrial protocols, or prefer a Java ecosystem.

alternatives.name: Home Assistant
alternatives.text: openHAB's architecture enforces cleaner separation of concerns but has fewer integrations and a smaller community. Home Assistant is more approachable for most users.

alternatives.name: Node-RED
alternatives.text: openHAB handles device bindings and state natively; Node-RED handles flow-based logic. They pair well together (openHAB exposes items via REST API to Node-RED).

entries.name: Node-RED
prose: Flow-based visual programming tool built on Node.js. In the IoT and home automation context, Node-RED excels at wiring together MQTT brokers, HTTP APIs, WebSocket streams, serial devices, and home automation hubs. Thousands of community nodes cover GPIO, Zigbee bridges, Telegram bots, database writes, and protocol translation.
> **Note:** Node-RED also appears in the Automation category for general workflow/integration use. This entry focuses on its IoT and smart home role.
entries.pick: you need a visual glue layer between IoT protocols, want to prototype device logic fast, or need to bridge systems that don't natively talk to each other (MQTT ↔ HTTP ↔ WebSocket ↔ serial).

alternatives.name: Home Assistant
alternatives.text: Node-RED is a logic/flow engine, not a device management platform. Many users run Node-RED as a companion to Home Assistant (via the `node-red-contrib-home-assistant-websocket` palette) for complex automations that outgrow HA's native automation editor.

alternatives.name: openHAB
alternatives.text: Node-RED is lighter and more flexible for arbitrary integrations; openHAB provides structured device/state management. Node-RED complements openHAB via its REST API.

categories.label: Media Management
categories.description: Media library automation, downloading, organizing, and metadata management

entries.name: Sonarr
prose: PVR for TV series. Monitors RSS feeds and indexers for new episodes, grabs them via Usenet or BitTorrent download clients, sorts and renames files, and upgrades quality when better releases appear. Integrates with Prowlarr for indexer management.
entries.pick: you want automated TV show downloading with quality profiles, season packs, calendar tracking, and automatic library organization.

alternatives.name: Radarr
alternatives.text: Sonarr is TV-only; Radarr is the same concept but for movies. Use both together for a complete library.

alternatives.name: Medusa/SickChill
alternatives.text: Sonarr has a modern UI, better API, active development, and tighter integration with the *arr ecosystem. Medusa/SickChill are legacy alternatives with dwindling communities.

entries.name: Radarr
prose: Movie collection manager for Usenet and BitTorrent. Monitors watchlists and RSS feeds for new movies, interfaces with download clients and indexers to grab, sort, and rename them. Supports quality profiles, custom formats, and automatic upgrades.
entries.pick: you want automated movie downloading with wishlists, quality upgrades, custom formats for preferred releases, and integration with Plex/Jellyfin/Emby.

alternatives.name: Sonarr
alternatives.text: Radarr is movies; Sonarr is TV. Fork of Sonarr adapted for movie workflows (no seasons/episodes, different metadata sources). Use both together.

alternatives.name: CouchPotato
alternatives.text: CouchPotato is abandoned. Radarr is the direct spiritual successor with active development, better UI, and broader integration.

entries.name: Prowlarr
prose: Indexer manager and proxy for the *arr stack. Manages both torrent trackers and Usenet indexers in one place, syncing them to Sonarr, Radarr, Lidarr, and Readarr. No per-app indexer configuration needed — add once in Prowlarr and sync everywhere.
entries.pick: you run multiple *arr apps and want centralized indexer management with automatic sync, or if you want to search across all indexers from a single UI.

alternatives.name: Jackett
alternatives.text: Prowlarr is the modern replacement. Native *arr integration (auto-sync indexers), built on the same stack, supports Cardigann definitions. Jackett still works but requires manual per-app indexer setup and doesn't sync configuration.

alternatives.name: NZBHydra2
alternatives.text: NZBHydra2 is Usenet-only; Prowlarr handles both Usenet and torrents. Prowlarr has tighter arr-stack integration. NZBHydra2 has better search statistics if you only use Usenet.

entries.name: Bazarr
prose: Companion application to Sonarr and Radarr for automated subtitle management. Monitors your library, searches multiple subtitle providers (OpenSubtitles, Addic7ed, Subscene, etc.), downloads matching subtitles, and keeps them synced as your library changes. Supports multiple languages, hearing-impaired subtitles, and forced subtitles.
entries.pick: you watch content in multiple languages or want automatic subtitle downloads without manual searching. Essential if your library serves non-English speakers.

alternatives.name: manual subtitle downloads
alternatives.text: Bazarr automates the entire workflow: matching, downloading, renaming, and re-downloading if a better subtitle appears or your media file changes.

alternatives.name: Jellyfin/Plex built-in subtitle search
alternatives.text: Media servers can search for subtitles on-demand but don't pre-download or monitor. Bazarr ensures subtitles are ready before you hit play.

categories.label: Media
categories.description: Media servers, music streaming, podcast management, and ebook libraries

entries.name: Jellyfin
prose: Free and open-source media server. Movies, TV, music, books, photos, live TV. No accounts, no tracking, no premium tiers.
entries.pick: you want a fully free media server with no paywalled features and active community development.

alternatives.name: Plex
alternatives.text: Jellyfin if you want no cloud dependency, no account requirement, fully free; Plex if you want polish, mobile apps, and don't mind the account/paywall.

alternatives.name: Emby
alternatives.text: Jellyfin is the community fork of Emby from before it went proprietary. Pick Jellyfin unless you specifically need an Emby-only feature.

entries.name: Plex
prose: Polished media server with excellent client apps across all platforms. Requires a free Plex account; some features (hardware transcoding, downloads) locked behind Plex Pass (~$5/mo or $120 lifetime).
